metadata.title: PISA 2012 Results: Creative Problem Solving (Volume V) (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA 2012 volume reports results from a complex, multi-stage sampling design of 15-year-old students within participating countries and economies. The report describes strict technical standards for the PISA target population and exclusion rates, but the provided excerpt does not specify the exact student sampling weight variable names or any replicate-weight scheme. For analyses using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the official PISA student/sampling weights supplied in the dataset to obtain population-representative estimates and correct standard errors under the complex design. Because this volume is a descriptive benchmarking report (not an ML model-training paper), it does not require ML-specific handling of weights; however, any re-analysis should use the dataset’s provided weights and replicate weights (if available) to match PISA’s variance estimation approach.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The excerpt does not document a specific plausible-values (PV) strategy for the problem-solving scale, nor does it describe a concrete missing-data handling method for the analytic models reported in this volume. Instead, it provides general Reader’s Guide conventions for missing table entries (e.g., categories not applicable, too few observations, data not available/withdrawn). This indicates that the volume’s results are presented as scaled proficiency and proficiency-level summaries rather than as an explicitly documented PV-based modeling workflow in the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The volume reports PISA 2012 problem-solving results for the PISA target population of 15-year-olds (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) enrolled in school and having completed at least 6 years of formal schooling. The excerpt states that overall exclusion rates within a country were required to be below 5% (and typically below 2–5% across most countries) to limit distortion of national mean scores; exclusions could occur at the school level (e.g., remote/inaccessible or very small schools) or at the student level (e.g., intellectual disability or limited proficiency in the assessment language). The provided text does not specify additional analytic subsample restrictions specific to the problem-solving volume (e.g., particular modules or grade filters), so the analytic sample is treated as the full available PISA 2012 problem-solving participant sample for the countries/economies covered in this volume.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2012 Volume V reports students’ problem-solving competence assessed on computer, focusing on interactive problem solving and general cognitive processes. The assessment was administered to about 85,000 students in 44 participating countries and economies, with results reported on a problem-solving proficiency scale and proficiency levels (e.g., top performers at Level 5 or 6). The report provides benchmarking across countries/economies, including mean scores, shares of low achievers and top performers, and relative performance compared with students with similar mathematics, reading and science performance. It also describes how performance varies by problem-solving processes and by the nature of problem situations (static vs interactive; knowledge acquisition vs utilisation). The excerpt does not document an ML prediction pipeline; instead, it presents scaled outcomes and statistically significant differences, and it cautions that PISA cannot identify direct cause-and-effect relationships between policies and student outcomes.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA results volume that synthesizes descriptive benchmarking and subgroup comparisons rather than training or evaluating machine-learning predictive models. As a result, there are no ML algorithms, PV-handling choices, or missing-data imputation strategies explicitly documented in the provided excerpt, and the extraction therefore leaves main_findings empty per the schema rules for official assessment/report volumes. The report does provide general Reader’s Guide conventions for missing table entries and describes the PISA target population and exclusion-rate requirements, which are used here to characterize the assessment design rather than to populate ML-specific fields.
